claims.claim: NCA-reported seizures include 21 boats and 24 engines in Germany (4 Dec 2024); 25 inflatables of about 8 m 'typically' used to carry 50-60 people each at Kapitan Andreevo, Bulgaria (26 Jul 2025); more than 30 boats, more than 20 engines, 360 pumps and more than 9,000 life jackets in North Rhine-Westphalia, some packed as 'go kits' of boat, engine, pump and fuel (21 May 2026); 25 inflatables at Lesovo, Bulgaria (24 and 26 Jun 2026); and 25 ten-metre boats with 25 Parsun engines in a container shipped from China, seized at Felixstowe en route to Hamburg (18 Jul 2026), each boat estimated to carry about 80 people.
claims.confidence_rationale: Each figure is the NCA's direct report of its own operation; the capacity figures are NCA estimates, not measurements.

geography.scope: Supply routes in Bulgaria, Germany and the UK (transit)

claims.limitations: Selected, publicised seizure batches; not a sample of boats used in crossings.

claims.claim: Official cumulative counts of seized equipment combine boats and engines and differ in scope: 'more than 600 boats and engines in the last 18 months' (NCA, 17 Apr 2025); 'more than 650 boats and engines since early 2023' (NCA, 31 Jul 2025); 'more than 950 boats and engines seized since early 2023' (GOV.UK, 28 Jan 2026); 533 items of small boat equipment in 2025 (BSC report); 'more than 1,000 boats and engines since early 2023, with more than 500 seized in 2025' (NCA, 1 Jul 2026); 'more than 1,500 boats and engines' intercepted by the NCA and international partners since early 2023 (NCA, 22 Jul 2026); 1,100 boats and engines seized since the July 2024 election (Home Office, 25 Aug 2026).
claims.confidence_rationale: Direct official statements, but the boat/engine split, definitions (seized vs intercepted; NCA vs partners) and baselines vary, so the figures cannot be reconciled into a series.

evidence.locator: Paragraph beginning 'The work of our National Crime Agency'
Upstream section: '533 items of small boat equipment'

claims.limitations: The jump from >1,000 (1 Jul 2026) to >1,500 (22 Jul 2026) cannot be explained by the 25+25 Felixstowe items alone; the scope wording differs. Do not chart as a time series.

claims.claim: The NCA describes 'go kits' (inflatable boat, pumps, engine and, in the May 2026 case, fuel) assembled at storage sites in Germany, each worth over €10,000 and suitable for one launch; inner tubes used in place of life jackets entered via Italy (March 2025); seven vehicles carrying kits were intercepted in Belgium between April and December 2025, plus five in France and two each in Germany and the Netherlands; petrol cans were among items seized in North Rhine-Westphalia raids on 25 March 2026.
claims.confidence_rationale: Direct NCA accounts of its own investigations.
claims.limitations: No fuel quantities or engine specifications given.

claims.claim: The NCA's estimate that 25 boats seized in Bulgaria in June 2026 could have carried 'more than 1,700 people' implies a planning assumption of at least about 68 people per boat, compared with 'typically' 50-60 people per 8 m boat in its July 2025 Bulgarian seizure statement and about 80 per 10 m boat in July 2026.
claims.confidence_rationale: Simple division of two NCA-published figures; the output is an NCA planning assumption, not an observed load, and the 1,700 is a lower bound.

geography.scope: Seizure batches destined for the Channel

claims.limitations: The estimates' basis is unpublished; boat length for the 2026 Bulgarian batch is not stated.

claims.claim: The Government states that in 2025 'more than 60% of all engines used by smuggling gangs were found to be branded as Chinese manufactured engines' and that inflatable dinghies are 'often made using parts sourced in China'.
claims.confidence_rationale: Official press release; the basis (engines recovered, seized or observed) and denominator are not published.
claims.limitations: 'Branded as' Chinese is not proof of manufacture; the headline's 'more than half ... manufactured in China' is looser than the body text.

claims.claim: Officials describe Channel boats as under-powered rather than more powerful: an NCA Deputy Director (March 2026) spoke of '70 or more people crammed on, propelled by a hugely under-powered engine'; an NCA Branch Commander (July 2026) referred to 'under-powered engines'; the Cranston Inquiry (February 2026) describes 'a small outboard motor capable only of slow speeds'.
claims.confidence_rationale: Consistent attributed characterisations from official sources, with no engine-power figures.
claims.limitations: Qualitative; no horsepower data verified for any year.

claims.claim: CPS releases on 2026 endangerment prosecutions record boats with more than 70 people (17 Jan 2026), 74 people (73 others plus pilot, 9 Apr 2026), 67 people on a boat the prosecution said 'was designed to carry 20 passengers' (18 Apr 2026), 83 people (82 others plus pilot, 21 Jun 2026; notes to editors list 84) and 96 people (95 others plus pilot, 23 Jun 2026).
claims.confidence_rationale: Phase 2 review: prosecution records are primary sources under methodology.md; loads are as stated in court releases.

evidence.locator: Case list and notes to editors

claims.limitations: Only pilots charged under a new offence; the 'designed for 20' figure is the prosecution's statement about one boat, not a certified rating. Statements such as 'designed for 20 people' are the prosecution's assertions.

claims.claim: A Home Office news story records a crossing on 15 August 2023 in which a dangerously overcrowded dinghy carried 52 migrants, with passengers forced to stand on makeshift flooring.
claims.confidence_rationale: Official account of a conviction.
claims.limitations: Single case; no dimensions.

claims.claim: On 1 May 2024 a French gendarmerie vessel rescued 66 people from a migrant boat in difficulty off Dieppe (Seine-Maritime) and landed them at Dieppe.
claims.confidence_rationale: Content read from a local capture of a primary French maritime notice, but the notice URL is unverified.
claims.limitations: Single incident; no boat dimensions; URL to be resolved.

claims.claim: On 22 July 2026 a migrant boat put to sea off Yport (Seine-Maritime), suffered an engine failure but continued under French monitoring through the night, and at dawn on 23 July came to the beach at Berck-sur-Mer (Pas-de-Calais) to take on more people, becoming 'particularly overloaded'.
claims.confidence_rationale: Primary French maritime-authority notice.

evidence.locator: Section 'Opérations d'assistance et de sauvetage au large de la Baie de Somme (80) et d'Yport (76)'

claims.limitations: Single incident. Shows a southern launch followed by a coastal transit and pickup further north, not a direct long crossing.

claims.claim: A migrant boat whose departure was reported in the Veules-les-Roses sector (Seine-Maritime) on 3 August 2026 was monitored through the day and night; on the morning of 4 August, while still in the French search-and-rescue region near the UK region, its engine caught fire and the boat rapidly lost integrity; 173 people were rescued in total and landed at Boulogne-sur-Mer.
claims.confidence_rationale: Primary French maritime-authority notice.
claims.limitations: Single incident; boat length and fuel not stated; whether passengers were picked up along the coast is not stated.

claims.claim: On the night of 5-6 September 2026 a boat carrying about 140 migrants was reported to CROSS Jobourg west of the Baie de Seine; French vessels monitored it and it continued towards the UK. The Préfecture maritime described such a departure as unusual for the area.
claims.confidence_rationale: Primary French maritime-authority notice.
claims.limitations: Single incident; boat type/length, departure beach and arrival not stated in the notice.

claims.claim: Local French media reported that the ~140-person boat left from Utah Beach (Sainte-Marie-du-Mont, Manche), according to the mayor, and arrived at Eastney, Portsmouth on the evening of Sunday 6 September 2026, a crossing of roughly 24 hours.
claims.confidence_rationale: News report with named local attribution, consistent with the Préfecture maritime notice; the UK arrival point is not officially confirmed in retrieved sources.
claims.limitations: Single event; do not treat as a route pattern.

claims.claim: The straight-line distance between Utah Beach and Eastney, Portsmouth is about 153 km (82 nm), compared with the MAIB-derived ~3 kn speed of one overloaded boat in 2022; at 3 kn the straight line alone would take about 27 hours.
claims.confidence_rationale: Phase 2 review: endpoints from news reports; the speed comes from a different boat.
claims.limitations: Illustrative arithmetic only; speed from a different boat and year. Conflicts with 156.6 km in route-analysis.json (different endpoint coordinates); reconcile before use. Do not show the 27-hour figure.

claims.claim: French media attribute to the SNSM a record of 230 people on one boat on the night of 9-10 August 2026, and quote the SNSM Berck-sur-Mer station director as saying vessels of 15 m are increasingly seen.
claims.confidence_rationale: Second-hand via news; no Préfecture maritime or UK official notice with the count or boat dimensions was retrieved; the 15 m remark is an unmeasured observation.
claims.limitations: Record events are selected for attention; 15 m is not corroborated by any measurement in this pass.

claims.claim: The Border Security Commander's 2025-26 report states that criminal groups 'have adapted by using bunkering and storage facilities to deliver SBE just-in-time, while making the most of available supplies by dangerously overloading vessels', that 'intelligence indicated a sharp reduction in equipment flows in early 2025', and that groups tested new supply routes to avoid Bulgarian controls.
claims.confidence_rationale: An official causal interpretation linking overloading to equipment supply constraints; no supporting data published.

evidence.locator: Outcome section on France/near neighbours; Savas case study; Bulgarian SBE case study

claims.limitations: Attributed explanation; it competes with demand, revenue and enforcement explanations.

claims.claim: The NCA's 2026 National Strategic Assessment states that despite a 3% fall in small boat events in 2025, 'organised crime groups increased the number of migrants per boat to enable more arrivals'.
claims.confidence_rationale: Attributed intelligence assessment of intent; the arithmetic (fewer boats, more people) is official, the motive is interpretation.
claims.limitations: Describes loading per boat and says nothing about boat dimensions.

claims.claim: The Migration Observatory writes that more people per boat 'reflects the use of larger boats, but may also indicate that some boats are used beyond their capacity'.
claims.confidence_rationale: Research-institute interpretation with no cited vessel data.
claims.limitations: No measurements; both explanations are offered.

claims.claim: An InfoMigrants analysis (12 August 2026) concludes that 'individual boats are not necessarily becoming larger in every case, but the number of people being crammed into them has risen substantially'.
claims.confidence_rationale: Journalistic synthesis without primary vessel data; recorded only as a contrary interpretation.
claims.limitations: Not evidence in itself.

claims.claim: The Border Security Commander describes arrivals 'often arriving with fuel burns and hypothermia' from 'flimsy and unseaworthy boats', and says the boats are 'extremely fragile and overloaded' with a risk of collapse if intercepted away from shore.
claims.confidence_rationale: Attributed official characterisation; no injury statistics published.

evidence.locator: Commander's foreword; operating context; maritime section

claims.limitations: Shows fuel is carried and spilt in the boats; says nothing about fuel quantity or range.

claims.claim: On the evidence retrieved, carrying load per boat has clearly increased; boats also appear somewhat larger at the upper end (from about 7.5-8 m in 2021 to 8-10 m typical, with 10 m seized batches in 2026; boats of up to 10 m were already reported in 2021), but boats of the same ~8 m class are reported with much heavier loads. An increase in operational range, engine power or fuel capacity is not established.
claims.confidence_rationale: Phase 2 review: the occupancy component is covered by official statistics (HIGH, see OCCUPANCY-*); the size component rests on one Cranston evidence item with no stated method (VES-CRANSTON-LENGTH) and selected seizure reports, so LOW; range is not established. MEDIUM borrowed credibility from the occupancy statistics.
claims.limitations: See research/crossings/vessel-findings.md for contradicting and missing evidence. Vessel observations come from seizures, prosecutions, incidents and news, not a representative sample. The 15 m remark (VES-SNSM-230-15M) is not evidence of a trend.

claims.claim: The Préfecture maritime's 2025 annual review states that 49,966 people aboard 795 boats attempted to cross the Channel from France to the United Kingdom in 2025.
claims.confidence_rationale: Directly stated in an official operational review, but the counting rule (attempts at sea vs launches vs boats detected; inclusion of prevented or returned boats) is not published, and '795' is used for boats on p.4 and for migrant operations on p.2.

evidence.locator: p.4 'Bilan sur la sécurité en mer', 'Phénomène migratoire': '49 966 personnes à bord de 795 embarcations qui ont tenté de traverser la Manche de la France vers le Royaume-Uni'; p.2 key figures '6 177 migrants au cours de 795 opérations'

geography.scope: France to UK attempts, Manche–mer du Nord façade

claims.limitations: Attempts are not UK arrivals (Home Office 2025 arrivals are a different measure; see ANNUAL-2025) and not launches by sector. No geographic distribution. A secondary report's '49,996' is not supported by the PDF.

claims.claim: The 2025 review reports 6,177 people rescued, and 25 deaths and 2 missing in search-and-rescue operations under the maritime prefect's responsibility, in the context of Channel crossing attempts in 2025.
claims.confidence_rationale: Directly stated; definitions of 'secourues' and the SRR scope of deaths are not given in the 2025 document (earlier reviews separate French and UK SRR deaths).

evidence.locator: p.4: '6 177 personnes ont été secourues. Malheureusement 25 sont décédées et 2 sont portées disparues dans le cadre des opérations SAR conduites sous la responsabilité du préfet maritime'

geography.scope: French SAR operations, Manche–mer du Nord

claims.limitations: Rescued people are mostly landed in France and are not UK arrivals; no location breakdown.

claims.claim: The 2025 review states that people per boat rose from 26 (2021) to 45 (2023) and 63 (2025), that 10 boats carried more than 100 people in 2025, and that 45% of boats in 2025 were 'taxi boats' — 8–10 m inflatables launched away from gathering areas that run along the coast to collect passengers near the shore.
claims.confidence_rationale: Directly stated but no method is given for per-boat averages or taxi-boat classification; earlier review vintages give different per-boat averages (GEO-FR-SERIES-REVISIONS).

evidence.locator: p.4 'Les risques ...': '(26 en 2021, 45 en 2023, 63 en 2025 ; cette année 10 embarcations transportaient plus de 100 personnes)'; 'en 2025, 45% des embarcations étaient des taxi-boats'; taxi-boat definition sentence

claims.limitations: Taxi-boat launch points are by definition away from pickup points: launch geography and loaded-crossing geography differ. Not a vessel-dimension series.

claims.claim: The Préfecture maritime's 2024 review tabulates migration-related maritime operations, people involved and people rescued: 2018 78/586/120; 2019 203/2,294/492; 2020 868/9,561/2,036; 2021 1,360/35,382/8,609; 2022 1,304/51,870/8,323; 2023 797/35,876/4,858; 2024 830/45,203/6,310.
claims.confidence_rationale: Directly tabulated in an official review; values differ from earlier vintages and column definitions changed between editions (GEO-FR-SERIES-REVISIONS).

evidence.locator: p.20 §3.2.5 table 'Nombre total d'opérations / Nombre de personnes impliquées / Nombre de personnes ayant été secourues'; footnote: SRR = CROSS Gris-Nez responsibility zone

geography.scope: CROSS Gris-Nez / Manche–mer du Nord façade

claims.limitations: Operational counts, not launches, and not sector-disaggregated; cannot support a dispersion analysis. Deaths: 2022 1 in FR SRR + 4 in UK SRR; 2023 11 dead, 2 missing FR SRR; 2024 72 dead, 3 missing FR SRR.

claims.claim: French annual-review vintages disagree: 2019 is 271 events/2,758 migrants in the 2019 review but 203/2,294 in the 2020–2024 reviews; 2020 people involved are 9,551 (2020–2023 reviews) vs 9,561 (2024 review); 2022 is 51,786 (2022–2023 reviews) vs 51,870 (2024 review); 2023 is 35,800 people, 12 dead, 4 missing, 6,450 rescued (2023 review) vs 35,876, 11, 2, 4,858 (2024 review); per-boat averages are 30 (2022) and 50 (2023) in the 2023 review vs 45 (2023) in the 2024–2025 reviews and 37 (2022) quoted from the prefect in 2025.
claims.confidence_rationale: Our side-by-side comparison of directly read values; every input is cited.

evidence.locator: p.5: 868 events, 9 551 migrants; 2019 recount '203 tentatives ou traversées impliquant 2294 migrants'; '6 décès et 3 disparus'
p.4 table (third column 'ayant fait un retour en France')
pp.15–16 text and table (51 786; column 'sauvées en mer')
p.14 table and text ('30 personnes en 2022 contre 50 personnes en 2023')
p.20 table and bullet ('45 migrants par embarcation en 2023, à 54 en 2024')
Quote attributed to Vice-amiral de Guibert: 'En 2022, il y avait en moyenne 37 migrants par embarcation, en 2024, c'était 54'

claims.limitations: Causes of revisions are not documented (beyond the 2020 statement that 2019 was recounted on the 2020 basis). Column meaning changed: 'retour en France' (2021), 'sauvées en mer' (2022), 'sauvées en mer et retour en France' (2023), 'secourues' (2024). Use one vintage per series and flag revisions. FR-REVIEW-2024 is also internally inconsistent (50,010 persons involved on p.6 vs 50,012 on p.9).

calculation.formula: value-by-value comparison of the same year's figures across French annual-review editions (inputs are the evidence locators)

values.note: Differences are between published editions; no figure is recalculated.

claims.claim: The 2024 review's key figures show 50,010 people involved in CROSS-coordinated operations in 2024, 46,330 in the CROSS Gris-Nez zone (annotated 'dont 45 203 migrants') and 3,680 in the CROSS Jobourg zone; in the Gris-Nez sector 72 of 82 deaths were linked to migration.
claims.confidence_rationale: Directly shown; the attribution of '45 203 migrants' to Gris-Nez rests on page layout, and p.9 gives 50,012 rather than 50,010.

evidence.locator: p.6 '2. Chiffres clés 2024' (Personnes impliquées panel); p.9 §3.2.1 ('Secteur CROSS Gris-Nez : 82 décès, dont 72 en lien avec le phénomène migratoire')

geography.scope: CROSS Gris-Nez vs CROSS Jobourg zones (boundary in Seine-Maritime per FR-REVIEW-2025 p.3 map)

claims.limitations: The Gris-Nez zone runs from the Belgian border into Seine-Maritime, so concentration within it cannot be resolved to Dunkirk/Calais/Boulogne/Somme/Seine-Maritime.

claims.claim: The Préfecture maritime's 2021 review states that departures took place mainly between Dunkirk and Calais but were extending increasingly south as far as Berck, with a few rare events observed towards Dieppe.
claims.confidence_rationale: Official qualitative operational summary; no counts by sector are published.

evidence.locator: p.4 boxed text: 'Les départs se font principalement entre Dunkerque et Calais, mais le phénomène s'étend de plus en plus vers le sud, pouvant aller jusqu'à Berck. Quelques rares évènements ont été observés vers Dieppe.'

claims.limitations: Qualitative; 'mainly' is unquantified. Evidence both for concentration (2021) and early southern spread.

claims.claim: The Préfecture maritime's 2024 review lists, among features of 2024 rescue operations, the extension of departure zones southwards as far as Dieppe.
claims.confidence_rationale: Official qualitative statement; no counts, dates or share of departures by sector.

evidence.locator: p.20 §3.2.5 bullet: 'L'extension des zones de départ vers le sud jusqu'à Dieppe'

claims.limitations: Seine-Maritime events were already documented in 2021 (GEO-SEINE-MARITIME-NOTICES, GEO-FR-2021-DEPARTURE-GEOGRAPHY), so the change is in frequency/salience, which is not quantified.

claims.claim: The 2024 review asserts that the southward extension of departure zones 'mechanically' lengthens crossing durations, exposing migrants longer to the elements and to overloading effects.
claims.confidence_rationale: Attributed official interpretation; plausible geometrically but no duration or distance data are provided, and taxi-boat pickups further north may shorten the loaded leg.

evidence.locator: p.20 §3.2.5 bullet: 'entraînant mécaniquement un allongement des durées des traversées'

claims.limitations: No crossing-duration series exists in the retrieved sources.

claims.claim: The 2021 French review attributes the first crossings (2016) to tighter security at the Channel Tunnel and ferry terminals and states that in 2018 this reinforced security initiated a shift of attempts to precarious boats spread along the coasts.
claims.confidence_rationale: Official causal interpretation without supporting analysis in the document.

evidence.locator: p.4: 'En 2018, cette sécurité renforcée a initié un déplacement des tentatives de traversées vers des embarcations précaires, réparties sur les côtes.'

claims.limitations: Route-substitution explanation; competing explanations belong in the Part 5 matrix.

claims.claim: The 2023 French review states that onshore internal-security action 'clearly' limits flows at sea but that smuggling networks adapt, so that each boat now carries more people.
claims.confidence_rationale: Official interpretation; no counterfactual or quantitative test provided.

evidence.locator: p.14 §3.2.5: 'Les actions des forces de sécurité intérieure conduites à terre permettent clairement de limiter les flux en mer. Mais les réseaux de passeurs ... s'adaptent aux contraintes'

claims.limitations: Relevant to Part 5 explanations; not a geographic measurement.

claims.claim: The 2022 French review states that figures and observations confirm boats were getting larger and carrying more people, with up to 70 people per boat on some days, a change it dates to after May 2022.
claims.confidence_rationale: Official qualitative observation; no dimensional data or method.

evidence.locator: p.16: 'Les chiffres et les observations confirment que embarcations s'agrandissent et embarquent plus de personnes ... jusqu'à 70 personnes ... qu'après le mois de mai 2022'

claims.limitations: For the vessel workstream; says nothing about range or route length. The same page notes larger boats are 'not necessarily safer'.

claims.claim: The Border Security Commander's 2025–26 report describes signs of potential geographic displacement, with some launches from beaches further south in France and a small number further north in Belgium.
claims.confidence_rationale: Attributed official assessment; no counts, dates or locations given.

evidence.locator: Threat context paragraph: 'There are also signs of potential geographic displacement with some launches occurring from beaches further south in France and a small number further north in Belgium.'

claims.limitations: 'Potential' and 'signs' are hedged; the report's inference that enforcement is making launches harder is in GEO-BSC-DISPLACEMENT-EXPLANATION.

claims.claim: The Border Security Commander interprets the southward and Belgian launches as a sign that enforcement is making launches more difficult but not preventing crossings.
claims.confidence_rationale: Attributed causal interpretation; evaluations are described as ongoing.

evidence.locator: Same paragraph: 'This suggests enforcement is making launches more difficult, but not preventing crossings altogether.'

claims.limitations: Complements existing BELGIUM-EXPLANATION; competing explanations (supply disruption, weather, demand) not tested.

claims.claim: According to a Belgian federal police spokesperson quoted by VRT on 25 March 2026, 15 boat departures from the Belgian coast had been recorded since early January 2026, compared with 0, 1 or at most 2 per year previously; departures were from Belgian beaches or the Nieuwpoort marina.
claims.confidence_rationale: Attributed official figure in an established public-broadcaster report; the Belgian police primary page could not be retrieved (HTTP 403/maintenance).

evidence.locator: Quote of An Berger: 'Er zijn sinds begin januari al 15 vertrekken van boten vastgesteld vanaf de Belgische kust ... In de jaren voordien waren er geen, 1 of maximaal 2 vertrekken per jaar.'
'In maart zijn er nog 14 vertrekken met bootjes geweest vanaf Belgische stranden, in april nu dus al 12.'

claims.limitations: Corroborates the BSC's Belgian examples (BELGIUM-2026) with Belgian official statements, at second hand. 'Departure' is not defined; many were taxi legs to French waters (GEO-BE-TAXI-TO-FRANCE). Figures across articles (15 by late March; 14 in March + 12 in April to 18 April) are not reconciled.

claims.claim: VRT reported that on 18 April 2026 five boats carrying about 200 people were intercepted off the Belgian coast between Oostduinkerke and Middelkerke and that police escorted them towards French waters.
claims.confidence_rationale: Established news report quoting the provincial governor; single report.

evidence.locator: Lead paragraph and Governor Decaluwé quote ('de bootjes zijn al begeleid naar Frankrijk')

geography.scope: Belgian coast between Oostduinkerke and Middelkerke

claims.limitations: Final destination of these boats unknown; they cannot be linked to UK arrivals.

claims.claim: The Westkust police chief described Belgian departures in early 2026 as taxi-boat operations: people wade out from lightly watched dunes at Oostduinkerke and Nieuwpoort, board boats that sail along the coast to France, and only then make the crossing.
claims.confidence_rationale: Attributed police description in an established news report; general, not per-event.

evidence.locator: Nico Paelinck quote: 'Ze komen bijvoorbeeld vanuit de duinen van Oostduinkerke en Nieuwpoort ... Pas als ze in Frankrijk zijn, maken ze dan de oversteek'

geography.scope: Belgian west coast (Koksijde/Oostduinkerke, Nieuwpoort, De Panne)

claims.limitations: Evidence against treating Belgian launches as longer direct Belgium–UK crossings. The article's claim that 'almost 4 in 5' reach England is an unverified police estimate and is not used.

claims.claim: VRT reported on 3 June 2026 that no migrants had been seen off the Belgian coast and no police interventions had taken place since 1 May 2026, after 33 boat interventions earlier in 2026 in which 426 people (34 minors) were checked.
claims.confidence_rationale: Established news report citing federal police and the Migration Minister; primary Belgian data not retrieved.

evidence.locator: Lead: 'Sinds 1 mei zijn er geen transmigranten meer gezien voor onze kust en geen politie-interventies meer geweest'; 'In totaal zijn er dit jaar 33 interventies geweest met bootjes aan onze kust ... 426 mensen gecontroleerd, van wie 34 minderjarigen'

claims.limitations: Evidence against a sustained northward expansion: the Belgian episode appears concentrated in roughly January–April 2026. Status after 3 June 2026 not checked.

claims.claim: VRT reports that the arrest in late March 2026 in Germany of four suspected suppliers of boats, engines and lifejackets (on the instruction of a Bruges investigating judge) reportedly helped cut the supply of nautical equipment to the Belgian coast.
claims.confidence_rationale: Hedged ('zou') causal attribution in a news report; no supporting data; timing (late March arrests, activity until end of April) is only loosely consistent.

evidence.locator: 'De arrestatie van 4 mensen in Duitsland zou er mee voor gezorgd hebben ...'; 'In opdracht van de onderzoeksrechter in Brugge zijn eind maart in Duitsland 4 personen gearresteerd'

claims.limitations: Lead for the Part 5 explanation matrix (supply-chain disruption); corroboration needed.

claims.claim: ICI (Radio France), citing the Préfecture de la Seine-Maritime, reported 19 prevented departure attempts in Seine-Maritime in 2025 up to 20 August (455 migrants found on land), compared with 5 onshore interventions (111 people) and 4 attempts that failed after breakdowns (87 people) in the whole of 2024.
claims.confidence_rationale: Attributed prefecture figures in an established public-broadcaster report; primary prefecture release not retrieved; categories differ between years.

evidence.locator: 'Depuis le début de l'année 2025, 19 tentatives de départs ont été empêchées en Seine-Maritime. Cela représente 455 migrants'; 'Sur toute l'année 2024, 5 interventions à terre ... 111 personnes, et 4 tentatives ont échoué ... 87 personnes, indiquent les services de la préfecture'

geography.scope: Seine-Maritime (76), between Le Tréport and Dieppe

claims.limitations: The only département-level count found. Partial year vs full year; prevented departures only (the article notes crossings that reached England are not included). Cannot be combined with other départements.

claims.claim: Préfecture maritime notices document migrant boats off Seine-Maritime on 9 March 2021 (off Berneval-le-Grand, 33 landed at Dieppe), 1 May 2024 (off Dieppe, 66 landed at Dieppe), 28 September 2025 (off Dieppe), 15 June 2026 (reported by the Dieppe semaphore, 30 landed at Boulogne) and 22 July 2026 (off Yport).
claims.confidence_rationale: Each occurrence is directly recorded in a primary official notice.

evidence.locator: 'Vers 04h30 du matin, le CODIS 76 signale ... au large de Dieppe'
'Une seconde embarcation est signalée par le sémaphore de Dieppe (76)'

claims.limitations: Selected notices found by targeted search; they establish occurrence since at least 2021, not frequency or trend. Launch sites are often not stated.

claims.claim: Préfecture maritime notices document departures or embarkation attempts on the Somme coast and southern Pas-de-Calais in December 2024 (boat stranded at Saint-Valery-sur-Somme), February and March 2025 (Baie de Somme launches, with an embarkation attempt at Berck and a stranding at Hardelot), June 2026 (Cayeux-sur-Mer sector) and July 2026 (Baie de Somme).
claims.confidence_rationale: Each occurrence is directly recorded in a primary official notice.

evidence.locator: Final operation paragraph (Baie de Somme / Berck)
'Enfin, une opération ... parti le matin au large de la Baie de Somme'
'le départ d'une embarcation depuis le secteur de Cayeux-sur-Mer (80)'
'au large de la Baie de Somme (80)'

claims.limitations: Occurrence only; several Somme launches were followed by pickups or strandings further north (Berck, Hardelot).

claims.claim: Préfecture maritime notices from 2025–2026 record departures, rescues or strandings along the whole Nord–Pas-de-Calais coast, including Leffrinckoucke, Malo-les-Bains, Petit-Fort-Philippe, Gravelines, the Walde lighthouse, Cap Blanc-Nez, Wimereux, Equihen, Écault and Hardelot, and often describe partial rescues after which the remaining occupants continued towards the UK.

claims.claim: The Home Office 'red day' measure is a Met Office daily Red-Amber-Green assessment of the likelihood that at least one small-boat crossing is attempted in the Dover Strait. It does not consider vessel availability or estimate volume, and its baselines were updated in April 2023 to reflect a sustained increase in crossing behaviour.
claims.confidence_rationale: Directly supported by the cited source within the stated scope. Methodological definition published with the official statistic.
claims.limitations: Because recent crossing trends and behaviour-based baselines are inputs, red-day counts are not an exogenous weather index. They cannot separate weather from enforcement, supply, demand or tactics, and a red-day count partly reflects the behaviour it is used to explain.

claims.confidence_rationale: Attributed interpretation from the cited source; supported as a statement of that source's view, not as an independently identified causal effect. Intelligence assessment using probabilistic language.
claims.limitations: Not an independent causal analysis. The NCA attributes fewer 2025 fatalities to rescue craft and fewer non-paying passengers storming boats.

claims.claim: A Border Forensics / University of Bristol investigation reports a surge in fatal incidents from summer 2023 while dinghy and arrival numbers fell. Its analysis of French coastguard location data puts these deaths closer to French shores. It attributes them to extreme overcrowding and chaotic launches, driven by supply-chain disruption (leading facilitators to source larger, lower-quality inflatables), aerial surveillance and UK-funded French policing, which it says 'altered the geography of small boat departures' and drove the adoption of taxi boats.
claims.confidence_rationale: Phase 2 review: advocacy analysis; the full report and its location analysis were not verified.
claims.limitations: Full report and datasets not reviewed; the location analysis is not independently verified.

claims.claim: Border Forensics argues that Home Office people-per-boat averages, being derived from arrivals, may underestimate how crowded boats are on departure.
claims.confidence_rationale: Plausible measurement argument by one source; no quantification seen.
claims.limitations: Direction of bias is argued, not measured. People rescued or intercepted before arrival are excluded from UK occupancy (see DEFINITION-ARRIVALS).

claims.claim: The Migration Observatory summarises studies showing that Channel smuggling runs as loose, localised networks rather than hierarchical gangs, with replaceable members and low barriers to entry, so high demand gives strong incentives for new actors to fill gaps left by enforcement.
claims.confidence_rationale: Attributed interpretation from the cited source; supported as a statement of that source's view, not as an independently identified causal effect.

evidence.locator: What measures have been proposed to reduce small boat arrivals?

claims.limitations: Underlying studies not individually read in this pass.

claims.claim: The Mixed Migration Centre concludes that stricter policies on the Channel and other routes have produced increasingly adaptive and professionalised smuggling rather than cutting supply, and that there is little evidence that deterrence policies deter irregular movement.
claims.confidence_rationale: Qualitative multi-route synthesis; Channel evidence is thin.
claims.limitations: Not a causal test.

claims.claim: The Migration Observatory reports uncertain evidence that crossing prices fell from around €14,000 in 2018 to well under €4,000 by 2024, with media investigations indicating around €1,500 in early 2026.
claims.confidence_rationale: Estimates the source itself calls uncertain, from media and NGO reports.

evidence.locator: How did the small boat route across the Channel emerge?

claims.limitations: Prices vary by nationality (see EXP-DNPAF-PROFILE-PRICE) and service; not a price series.

claims.claim: In the year ending June 2026, the most common small-boat nationalities were Eritrean (5,875, down 2% on the previous year), Sudanese (4,191, up 11%), Afghan (down 37%), Somali (3,901, up 76%) and Iranian (down 15%). Together these five made up two-thirds of arrivals.
claims.confidence_rationale: Directly supported by the cited source within the stated scope.
claims.limitations: Excludes arrivals whose nationality is not yet recorded.

claims.claim: Detected illegal entry by method, 2018 to 2025: small-boat arrivals rose from 299 to 45,774 (2022) and were 41,472 in 2025. Recorded detections in the UK fell from 7,257 (2018) and 8,492 (2019) to 1,816 (2025). Recorded detections at UK ports fell from 1,052 to 204, and inadequately documented air arrivals went from 4,769 to 3,016.
claims.confidence_rationale: Directly supported by the cited source within the stated scope.
claims.limitations: Detections, not entries: detection rates differ by method (see EXP-HO-METHOD-CAVEAT), so the series cannot show one-for-one substitution.

claims.claim: The Home Office advises against directly comparing detection numbers across entry methods, because the share detected varies by method. It says the post-2020 decline in other methods was likely due in part to COVID-19 making air and ferry entry less viable, and that small boats, as the most visible method, are the most likely to be detected and remained high as other routes became viable again.
claims.confidence_rationale: Attributed interpretation from the cited source; supported as a statement of that source's view, not as an independently identified causal effect. Official interpretation accompanying the statistics.
claims.limitations: The COVID explanation is not quantified.

claims.claim: The Home Affairs Committee concluded it is 'likely that some of the increase in small boat crossings is driven by tightened security on other methods'. It noted that clandestine entries stayed roughly constant in 2019-2020 while the small-boat share rose from 11% to 50%, and that this 'may suggest' security in northern France is displacing traffic into small boats.
claims.confidence_rationale: Attributed interpretation from the cited source; supported as a statement of that source's view, not as an independently identified causal effect. Committee inference from share data.
claims.limitations: A share shift is compatible with substitution but also with differential detection and COVID freight disruption.

claims.claim: The Chief Inspector reported in November 2020 that the Home Office attributed the late-2018 small-boat surge to enhanced port security, but judged that 'the evidence for this is inconclusive'. 'Lorry drop' migrants encountered in the UK rose by a third in 2019, and the 2016-2017 fall in Calais clandestine encounters (33,807 to 15,457) could not be separated from the October 2016 clearance of the Calais camp.
claims.confidence_rationale: Attributed evaluative judgement by an independent inspectorate; the figures are as reported in the inspection.
claims.limitations: Contradicts a simple displacement story for 2018-2019; later data (IER_01) show falls in other detected methods from 2020.

claims.claim: French interior ministry (DGEF) figures in the French inquiry report show land-route interceptions falling from 57,137 (2016) to 3,217 (2025). Estimated maritime attempts rose from none in 2016 to nearly 80,000 in 2022 and 63,899 in 2025. The report's Figure 1 note gives 22,427 for the maritime vector in 2025.
claims.confidence_rationale: Official figures relayed in a parliamentary report, with an internal inconsistency.

evidence.locator: Partie I.B.1, Figure 1 and text citing footnote 36

claims.limitations: Land figures count interceptions, not attempts or successes. The 22,427 value appears to match preventions (compare EXP-PREVENTED-SERIES) and the 63,899 value arrivals plus preventions (EXP-PREVENTED-SHARE). Use neither without reconciliation.

claims.claim: The French inquiry concludes that Franco-British agreements have not stopped crossing attempts but have displaced routes from lorries and the tunnel to more dangerous small boats and, more recently, taxi boats. It records the foreign ministry's legal director saying the securing of rail and port infrastructure 'led to' the small-boat and taxi-boat phenomenon.
claims.confidence_rationale: Attributed interpretation from the cited source; supported as a statement of that source's view, not as an independently identified causal effect. Parliamentary conclusion drawing on official testimony and DGEF data.
claims.limitations: Advocacy of the rapporteure's position; the conclusion was not unanimous in all respects.

claims.claim: Getlink (Eurotunnel) told the French inquiry that bad weather for sea crossings from November 2025 to March 2026, combined with stronger coastal security, led to renewed attempts to cross by lorry, with 40-60 interceptions a month.
claims.confidence_rationale: One operator's written answer relayed in the report; the causal link is the operator's view.
claims.limitations: Suggests substitution can run in reverse, but is a single short-period account.

claims.claim: A peer-reviewed analysis of 345 policy texts (Mayblin et al., 2024) states that by 2018 border measures had made lorry drops increasingly risky and unlikely to succeed, so people and smugglers adapted to small boats, and that boat use intensified during COVID-19 as less freight moved and smugglers charged more for lorry passage.
claims.confidence_rationale: Peer-reviewed, but the route-shift account is historical context drawn from secondary literature and inspectorate reports, not a tested causal finding.

evidence.locator: Section 'Fortifying the channel borderzone' (pp. 3-4 of article)

claims.limitations: Discourse-analysis paper; its main contribution concerns policy framing.

claims.claim: A peer-reviewed article (Davies et al., 2021) states that in 2020 Brexit border stoppages, industrial action at Calais and COVID-19 disrupted road haulage, reducing lorry and freight-train opportunities and increasing the likelihood of boat crossings.
claims.confidence_rationale: Peer-reviewed; supported by citations and 2015-2019 Calais fieldwork, not by a quantitative test.
claims.limitations: Covers 2020 only.

claims.claim: IPPR's stakeholders suggested that the shift to small boats was likely a combination of increased securitisation of other routes, the end of the UK's participation in the Dublin Regulation, and a 'snowball effect' from early success.
claims.confidence_rationale: Think-tank summary of stakeholder opinion.
claims.limitations: Opinion-based; no quantification.

claims.claim: The Illegal Migration Bill impact assessment states that it was 'not possible to estimate with precision the level of deterrence'. It cites an academic consensus of 'little to no evidence' that destination-country policy changes deter people from leaving or travelling without permission, while noting a stronger basis for effects on choice of destination and that displacement to other forms of illegal entry may weaken policy impacts.
claims.confidence_rationale: Attributed interpretation from the cited source; supported as a statement of that source's view, not as an independently identified causal effect. Government's own summary of the evidence base.
claims.limitations: Pre-implementation appraisal; not an evaluation.

claims.claim: The NAO reported that in April 2022 the Home Office Permanent Secretary could not conclude that the Rwanda policy would be value for money, because there was 'insufficient evidence' it would deter enough people. A ministerial direction was issued on 13 April 2022, and the NAO itself did not conclude on value for money because that rests on deterrence.
claims.confidence_rationale: Directly supported by the cited source within the stated scope.
claims.limitations: Cost investigation, not an impact evaluation.

claims.claim: Home Office-commissioned research on asylum seeker decision-making found 'insufficient evidence that restrictive asylum policies in the UK have an impact on the number of asylum seekers coming to the UK'. It found that social networks shape destination and timing, and that the availability of protection elsewhere in Europe is an important determinant of onward travel to the UK.
claims.confidence_rationale: Attributed interpretation from the cited source; supported as a statement of that source's view, not as an independently identified causal effect. Rapid evidence assessment of about 200 reports plus 29 stakeholder interviews.
claims.limitations: Asylum seekers were not interviewed. Predates the IMA, Rwanda and the returns pilot.

claims.claim: The Migration Observatory reports that no asylum seekers were forcibly relocated to Rwanda by the 2024 election. The scheme was cancelled by the Labour government, and most provisions of the Illegal Migration Act 2023 have been repealed by the Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Act, which became law in December 2025.
claims.confidence_rationale: Research synthesis; the primary legislation was not checked in this pass.

evidence.locator: What measures have been proposed to reduce small boat arrivals?

claims.limitations: Because the Rwanda and IMA removal mechanisms never operated at scale, their effect on crossings cannot be observed directly.

claims.claim: The Channel Crossings project report states that the deterrence aim of the Rwanda scheme was not shown to have had any material effect on arrivals while the scheme was being legislated and enacted.
claims.confidence_rationale: Interpretation in a non-peer-reviewed academic report by authors critical of the policy; no counterfactual analysis.
claims.limitations: Absence of an observed effect is not proof of no effect.

claims.claim: A peer-reviewed study of the Central Mediterranean, 2011-2020 (Rodríguez Sánchez et al., 2023), found using Bayesian structural time-series counterfactuals no discernible effect of state-led or NGO search-and-rescue periods on crossing attempts. The coordinated Libyan coastguard pushback period did affect the flow.
claims.confidence_rationale: Peer-reviewed causal-inference study, but for a different route.
claims.limitations: Transferability to the Channel, where UK and French rescue is routine and distances are short, is untested.

claims.claim: SCENARIO (not a forecast): REDUCTION assumes 256 arriving boats at 65.31 people per boat over an illustrative 12-month period, giving 16,720 modelled arrivals (-49.9% vs July 2025-June 2026).
claims.confidence_rationale: Hypothetical arithmetic on stated assumptions; confidence refers to the plausibility of the outcome, which is not assessed. The arithmetic itself is exact.

evidence.locator: IER_02a monthly and annual people and boats (anchors)

geography.scope: UK detected small-boat arrivals; origin not disaggregated

claims.limitations: Not a prediction. Occupancy is an average, not capacity. No departures, interceptions or routes are modelled. Says nothing about asylum support or where anyone lives.

claims.claim: The Commons Library reports that border officials say 'gangs are now using poorer quality boats, engines and fuel, which result in slower and more dangerous journeys with greater chances of failure.'
claims.confidence_rationale: An attributed official interpretation, reported by the Commons Library; no engineering data.
claims.limitations: Attributed interpretation; bears on H2 (range) but does not measure range.

claims.claim: A journalist's evidence to the French inquiry frames longer departures (e.g. from Brittany) as a logistics trade-off: 'quelques milliers d'euros d'essence en plus, quelques passagers en moins' (a few thousand euros more fuel, a few fewer passengers).
claims.confidence_rationale: A single attributed statement by a journalist; not official or engineering evidence.
claims.limitations: Speculative testimony; indicates range is framed as a fuel-versus-load choice, not a property of larger boats.

claims.claim: France's gendarmerie directorate (DGGN) told the French inquiry that, with the northern beaches better held, 'les migrants et les passeurs se sont reportés toujours plus au sud pour embarquer' (migrants and smugglers moved ever further south to embark).
claims.confidence_rationale: An official, attributed description consistent with French maritime reviews; qualitative, no counts.
claims.limitations: Describes the extent of the launch area and attributes it to enforcement; does not measure the distribution of departures.

claims.claim: The Cranston Inquiry found that on 23-24 November 2021 'HM Coastguard and Border Force were reluctant to deploy more than one, as this would have reduced the availability of an already insufficient number of assets on the following day.'
claims.confidence_rationale: Finding of a statutory inquiry, quoted verbatim.

geography.scope: UK search and rescue region, Dover Strait

claims.limitations: Refers to 2021 capacity; says nothing about route length (H4).

claims.claim: Cranston Inquiry Recommendation 3: 'There should be regular assessments by HM Coastguard of the adequacy of the available assets and human resources to respond to both current and reasonably foreseeable levels of small boat activity.'
claims.confidence_rationale: Recommendation text quoted verbatim.
claims.limitations: No assessment under this recommendation was found; the government response was not reviewed.

claims.claim: The Border Security Command reports that 'BSC Maritime is the main organisation tasked by Maritime and Coastguard Agency (MCA) to interdict and rescue migrants crossing the Channel (over 90% in FY25/26).'
claims.confidence_rationale: Statement in an official annual report, quoted verbatim.
claims.limitations: Share of taskings, not incident counts or response times; no breakdown by location.

classification_definitions.OFFICIAL_STATISTIC: A figure or definition published in official statistics.
classification_definitions.DOCUMENTED_EVENT: An event recorded in a primary official or investigative source.
classification_definitions.DERIVED_STATISTIC: Our calculation, with formula and input references.
classification_definitions.REPORTED_EVENT: An event or observation described second-hand or attributed (news, operational summaries).
classification_definitions.HYPOTHESIS: A proposed explanation, including officials' and researchers' causal interpretations.
classification_definitions.SCENARIO: Hypothetical assumptions and outputs; never observed data.

migration.from: schema_version 1 (OBSERVED FACT, DERIVED STATISTIC, REPORTED EVENT, HYPOTHESIS, SCENARIO; lower-case confidence)
migration.rule: OBSERVED FACT became OFFICIAL_STATISTIC for official statistics and definitions, or DOCUMENTED_EVENT for events recorded in primary official or investigative sources. REPORTED EVENT became DOCUMENTED_EVENT where the source is a primary official incident or investigation record, otherwise REPORTED_EVENT. Confidence levels were carried over unchanged and are reassessed in the Phase 2 critical review.
